title: Chemical Bonding
tagline: Transfer, sharing and donation of electrons, and how each bond type fixes the properties of a compound.

overview.intro: A bond exists because the joined system has lower energy than the separate atoms, and the way the electrons arrange themselves decides everything that follows. This chapter covers ionic bonding by transfer, covalent bonding by sharing, the coordinate bond where one partner supplies both electrons, VSEPR shapes from bond-pair and lone-pair repulsion, and the hydrogen bonding that gives water and DNA their special behaviour. The examination consistently asks the same two things: draw the electron arrangement correctly, then explain a physical property from the structure that produced it.

facts.label: Octet rule
facts.value: Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable outer shell of eight, or two for hydrogen.

facts.label: VSEPR
facts.value: Electron pairs around a central atom repel and take up positions of minimum repulsion.

facts.label: Hybridisation
facts.value: sp, sp^2 and sp^3 mixing gives linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral geometry.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Dot-and-cross diagrams, shapes and the properties comparison appear every year.

learningOutcomes: Show the formation of an ionic bond by electron transfer with a complete dot-and-cross account.
Describe covalent bonding and draw single, double and triple bonds between named atoms.
Explain the coordinate bond and give ammonium as a standard example.
Predict molecular shape and bond angle from VSEPR theory for named molecules and ions.
Classify a compound as ionic, metallic or covalent and justify its melting point, conductivity and solubility.

blocks.text: Ionic bonding happens when a metal with low ionisation energy meets a non-metal with high electron affinity: the metal transfers its valence electrons and becomes a cation, the non-metal receives them and becomes an anion, and the electrostatic attraction between opposite charges is the bond. Sodium chloride is the standard case, where sodium empties its 3s electron into chlorine’s 3p vacancy so that both reach a noble-gas arrangement. The product is not a molecule but a crystal lattice in which every ion is surrounded by six oppositely charged neighbours, and that structure explains the properties: high melting point because many strong attractions must be broken, hardness with brittleness because like-charged layers slide onto each other under a blow, and conductivity only when molten or dissolved because only then are the ions free to move.

items: Electrovalency equals the number of electrons transferred: sodium has electrovalency 1, magnesium 2.
Lattice energy, released as gaseous ions assemble into the crystal, makes formation exothermic overall.
Ionic solids conduct only when molten or in solution; the solid itself has no mobile charge.
Most ionic compounds dissolve in water, where ions become hydrated, and not in non-polar solvents.
Write the transfer in two steps — atom to ion — before adding them: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e−, then O + 2e− → O2−.

items.text: Sodium chloride: Na (2, 8, 1) → Na+ (2, 8), Cl (2, 8, 7) → Cl− (2, 8, 8)
items.note: Both ions reach the argon arrangement and the lattice assembles with 6 : 6 coordination.

items.text: Magnesium oxide: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e−, O + 2e− → O2−
items.note: Doubly charged ions give stronger attraction and a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.

blocks.caption: Ionic versus covalent behaviour
rows: Soft, gases or liquids at room temperature

blocks.text: When neither atom can take electrons outright they share a pair instead: one shared pair is a single bond, two a double bond and three a triple bond, and the count of pairs shared by an atom is its covalency. Sharing is rarely equal, because the more electronegative atom pulls the pair towards itself, which makes most bonds polar even though the molecule stays neutral. A coordinate bond is the special case in which both electrons of the pair come from the same atom: the donor contributes a lone pair and the acceptor an empty orbital, and once formed the bond is indistinguishable from any other single bond. This explains the ammonium ion, where three N–H bonds are ordinary and the fourth is coordinate in origin but identical afterwards, and it explains adducts such as H3N → BF3.

items: Hydrogen forms one bond, carbon four, nitrogen three, oxygen two, and the halogens one each.
A triple bond such as N≡N is short and very strong, which is why nitrogen is unreactive at room temperature.
Covalent compounds are held between molecules only by weak van der Waals forces, so they melt easily.
Coordinate bonding requires a lone pair on the donor and a vacant orbital or incomplete octet on the acceptor.
An arrow drawn from donor to acceptor marks the direction of the donation.

items.note: Nitrogen donates its lone pair; all four bonds are then identical and the ion carries one positive charge.
Boron has only six electrons around it and accepts nitrogen’s lone pair to complete its octet.

items.meaning: Number of electron pairs an atom shares in covalent bonding.
Shared pair in which both electrons come from one atom.
Non-bonding pair of electrons belonging to one atom.
Unequal sharing of a bonded pair, giving partial charges on the atoms.

blocks.text: VSEPR theory states that electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and take up the arrangement that minimises that repulsion, and that lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs. Two pairs give a linear molecule, three a trigonal planar shape, four a tetrahedron, five a trigonal bipyramid and an octahedron for six. The repulsion order lone pair : lone pair > lone pair : bond pair > bond pair : bond pair compresses the ideal angles, which is why water bends at 104.5° rather than the tetrahedral 109.5° and ammonia sits at 107°. Hybridisation explains the same shapes from the orbital side: mixing one s with one p orbital gives sp and a linear shape, with two p orbitals gives sp^2 and a trigonal planar shape, and with three p orbitals gives sp^3 and a tetrahedral shape.

items: Two electron domains → linear, 180°: BeCl2 and CO2.
Three domains → trigonal planar, 120°: BF3 and SO3.
Four domains → tetrahedral, 109.5°: CH4 and NH4+.
One lone pair on four domains → trigonal pyramidal, 107°: NH3; two lone pairs → bent, 104.5°: H2O.
Bond angles shrink as lone pairs are added because lone pair repulsion is the strongest of the three.

items.note: sp^3 carbon with four identical bond pairs gives a perfect tetrahedron at 109.5°.
Four domains, two of them lone pairs, give a bent molecule at 104.5° and a permanent dipole.

learn.title: Polarity, hydrogen bonding and structure to property

blocks.text: A polar bond makes a polar molecule only when the dipoles fail to cancel: carbon dioxide is linear and its two equal dipoles cancel, while water is bent and its dipoles reinforce. Polarity then decides physical behaviour. The strongest intermolecular attraction is the hydrogen bond, which occurs when hydrogen is bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, because those small, highly electronegative atoms leave the hydrogen nucleus almost bare to attract a lone pair on a neighbour. Hydrogen bonding explains water’s unusually high boiling point, the low density of ice, the viscosity of glycerol and the pairing of the bases in the DNA double helix. The general teaching rule stays the same throughout: identify the particles, identify the forces between them, and read the property off the forces.

items: Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules; dispersion forces act between all molecules and grow with size.
Hydrogen bonds form only with H bonded to N, O or F; an O–H group in an alcohol can hydrogen bond but the H of a C–H group cannot.
Ice floats because the hydrogen-bonded lattice holds molecules further apart than the liquid does.
Metallic bonding is positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, explaining conduction and malleability in the solid state.
High melting point plus molten conduction means giant ionic or metallic; low melting point plus no conduction means simple molecules.

items.text: Hydrogen chloride is a gas while sodium chloride melts at 801 °C
items.note: Both contain a polar bond, but one is a lattice of ions and the other separate molecules with only weak forces between them.
Its hydroxyl group hydrogen-bonds to water molecules, overcoming the hydrocarbon part’s reluctance to dissolve.

items.meaning: Attraction between an H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a neighbouring atom.
Product of charge separation and distance, measuring molecular polarity.
Weak attractions between molecules arising from temporary dipoles.
Metallic electrons not associated with any single atom and free to move.

keyPoints: Bonding lowers the energy of the joined system relative to separated atoms.
Ionic bonding is transfer from metal to non-metal, giving ions in a lattice.
Covalent bonding is sharing of electron pairs; single, double and triple bonds share one, two and three pairs.
A coordinate bond donates both electrons from one atom, as in NH4+.
VSEPR minimises repulsion between electron domains; lone pairs compress bond angles.
sp, sp^2 and sp^3 hybridisation give linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral geometries.
A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles fail to cancel in its shape.
Hydrogen bonding needs H directly bonded to N, O or F and explains water’s anomalous properties.
Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct only when molten or dissolved; covalent compounds do neither.
Metallic bonding, a sea of delocalised electrons, explains conduction and malleability in the solid state.
examFocus: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams with every electron shown and label the octet each atom achieves.
For property questions name the structure first, then the forces, then the observation; three parts, three marks.
Shape questions need the domain count, the lone-pair count and then the name and angle of the shape.
Learn the ionic versus covalent table with at least four contrasting rows and named examples.

Number of electrons an atom transfers to form an ionic bond.
Covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom.
Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion theory of molecular shape.
Mixing of atomic orbitals to give new equivalent hybrid orbitals of defined shape.
Angle between two bonds meeting at a central atom.
Weak attraction between an electropositive hydrogen and a lone pair on N, O or F.
Energy released when gaseous ions assemble into an ionic crystal.
A pair of equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance.
Spreading of electrons over more than two atoms or across a lattice.

questions.prompt: An ionic bond is formed by:
options: Sharing of electron pairs between two non-metals
Transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal
Sharing of a lone pair donated by one atom
questions.answer: Transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal
questions.explanation: Transfer creates oppositely charged ions whose electrostatic attraction constitutes the bond.

questions.prompt: Which substance is expected to have a high melting point and conduct electricity when molten?
questions.explanation: Only the ionic lattice has strong attractions between ions and releases mobile ions on melting.

questions.prompt: The shape of the ammonia molecule, with four electron domains of which one is a lone pair, is:
questions.explanation: Four domains give a tetrahedral arrangement, but with one lone pair the shape is trigonal pyramidal at about 107°.

questions.prompt: The bond angle in water is 104.5° rather than the tetrahedral 109.5° because:
options: Lone pair–lone pair and lone pair–bond pair repulsion are stronger than bond pair–bond pair repulsion
The oxygen atom is larger than carbon
Water has a double bond to one hydrogen
questions.answer: Lone pair–lone pair and lone pair–bond pair repulsion are stronger than bond pair–bond pair repulsion
questions.explanation: VSEPR ranks repulsion as lone pair : lone pair > lone pair : bond pair > bond pair : bond pair, so two lone pairs squeeze the angle.

questions.prompt: The number of electron pairs an atom shares in forming covalent bonds is called its __________ .
questions.explanation: Covalency counts shared pairs, while electrovalency counts electrons transferred.

questions.prompt: The regular three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions in an ionic crystal is called a crystal __________ .
questions.explanation: The lattice repeats the ion pattern in every direction and accounts for both the crystal shape and the brittleness.

questions.prompt: Define a coordinate bond and give one example.
questions.answer: A coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by one atom as a lone pair while the other atom supplies an empty orbital; the ammonium ion NH4+ contains one such bond formed when NH3 donates to H+.
questions.explanation: Once formed it is identical to an ordinary single bond, but the origin of the pair differs.

questions.prompt: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but the molten substance does.
questions.answer: Conduction requires mobile charged particles. In the solid lattice the Na+ and Cl− ions are fixed in position and can only vibrate, so no current flows. Melting breaks the lattice without breaking the ionic bonds, releasing ions that move under a potential difference and carry charge.
questions.explanation: The ions are present in both states; only their freedom to move differs.

questions.prompt: Using VSEPR, deduce the shape and bond angle of carbon dioxide and of the ammonium ion, and explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide has two double bonds and no lone pairs on carbon, giving two electron domains that repel to a linear shape with a bond angle of 180°. The ammonium ion has four bonding pairs around nitrogen and no lone pairs, because the fourth bond is a coordinate bond formed from nitrogen’s lone pair; four domains repel to a tetrahedral shape with an angle of 109.5°. In both cases the domain count, not the number of atoms bonded, sets the geometry.
questions.explanation: Count electron domains including multiple bonds as one domain each, then subtract nothing because neither central atom carries a lone pair.

questions.prompt: Explain why hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature while sodium chloride melts at 801 °C, even though both compounds contain a polar bond.
questions.answer: Hydrogen chloride consists of separate molecules in which the polar H–Cl bond creates only a dipole; between molecules act weak dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, so little energy separates them and the substance is gaseous. Sodium chloride is a giant lattice in which every ion is attracted strongly to six neighbours of opposite charge; melting must overcome many such interactions simultaneously, which requires 81 kJ per mole of ion pairs and gives a melting point of 801 °C. The polarity of an individual bond therefore says nothing about melting point; the structure and the forces between particles decide it.
questions.explanation: Melting behaviour follows what must be separated: molecules held by weak forces, or ions held in a lattice by electrostatic attraction.
